974.title: Nettles
974.hook: Milarepa lives on nettles in a cave until his skin turns green, singing songs
974.howItsDone: Tibetan paintings can show Milarepa with green-tinged skin and a hand cupped to his ear as he sings, and his songs are recited and studied in Kagyu communities and beyond.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the towers, built and torn down until Marpa took Milarepa as his student. Your line: build it again.

A thief creeps into a mountain cave at night, feeling along the walls for anything worth taking. In the dark, a voice starts laughing. It's the man who lives there, Milarepa, and he says something like: you're looking by night for what I can't find in the daytime. The thief finds nothing, because there is nothing. A cooking pot, perhaps. Some wild greens. Marpa has given Milarepa the teaching and sent him to the mountains to practice, and Milarepa has taken him at his word.
screen: `A THIEF IN THE CAVE.` → `A LAUGH IN THE DARK.` → `NOTHING TO TAKE.`

segments.voice: In his life story, Milarepa sits in caves far from any village, and the one thing growing near his door is nettles. He boils them and eats them, day after day, until, the story says, his body grows thin and his skin turns green. When people come by, some take him for a ghost. This isn't poverty he can't escape. It's simplicity he chose, so that nothing would pull him away from practice. Food was fuel, and nettles would do. Here's the surprise: Milarepa wasn't grim and silent in that cave. He sang. When hunters, his sister, old friends or skeptical scholars turned up, he answered them in songs, about impermanence, about his teacher's kindness, about the joy of the mountains. His songs are still sung and studied. So two pictures sit side by side: a man so thin he looks like a ghost, and a man so full he can't stop singing. The story doesn't treat that as a contradiction. Owning less made room for something. In the Life, this is the calling Marpa sent him to, one man's road after a hard training, not a menu for anyone else. What it offers is smaller: a meal that's just a meal, enough without the extra, and space left over for a song.
screen: `NETTLES, DAY AFTER DAY.` · `CHOSEN, NOT FORCED.` · `HE SANG.` · `THIN AS A GHOST, FULL OF SONG.` · then, large: `GREEN FROM NETTLES.`

segments.voice: Notice how little you need for these few minutes: a place to sit, air, a body that breathes, and let everything else wait outside the cave. With each out-breath, gently set down one want, a snack, a message, a plan, and see what's left.
Nettles. The wild greens Milarepa lived on in his cave, until, the story says, his skin turned green, while he sang. Today's word.
Your line: green from nettles. Thin as a ghost, and still singing in the cave. Till tomorrow.

975.title: The last teaching
975.hook: Milarepa shows his student Gampopa the callouses from years of sitting: that is the secret
975.howItsDone: Tibetan teachers tell the story of Milarepa's last teaching to Gampopa, often with humor, to stress that steady practice matters more than any secret instruction.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Milarepa in his cave, green from the nettles and singing anyway. Your line: green from nettles.

A goodbye at a river crossing. The old man has walked his student partway down the road. Gampopa has trained with him, and now he's being sent off to practice and teach on his own. They say their farewells, and the student bows. Then Milarepa calls him back. Wait, he says, in the story. I have one more instruction, a very precious one. I wasn't sure I'd give it to you. Gampopa turns around, ready for the deepest secret of all.
screen: `A GOODBYE AT THE RIVER.` → `WAIT. ONE MORE.` → `THE DEEPEST SECRET?`

segments.voice: Milarepa turns his back to Gampopa, hitches up his robe, and shows him his backside. It's covered in thick calluses, hard as hide, from sitting on stone for years. And he says, in effect: this is it. There's no instruction more profound than this. Practice. Sit until your seat looks like mine. It's funny, and it's meant to be. The singer of the mountains keeps his most precious teaching for last, and it's his rear end. It's hard to retell without a grin. Under the joke is the point. Everything Milarepa had, he got from teachings he received and then practiced, again and again, alone, in cold caves. The teaching mattered. But a teaching that isn't practiced is a map left folded in a drawer. The calluses are what reading the map looks like after years on the road. A student leaving a teacher wants a key, a secret, something to keep in a pocket. Milarepa gives Gampopa the opposite of a shortcut. The secret is that there's no secret, only the long sitting. Some hear good news in that: nothing is being held back, and there's no hidden password. There's only showing up, and showing up again. Tomorrow, the student who walked away from that river carrying it.

Milarepa. The singer of the mountains, whose parting gift to his student Gampopa was his calluses from years of sitting, and no secret beyond practice. Today's word.
Your line: that's the secret. No password, no shortcut, just the seat. Day nine hundred seventy-five, done.

976.title: Gampopa
976.hook: the doctor who became a monk and joined two streams in the Kagyu school
976.howItsDone: In the Kagyu school, Gampopa is honored as the one who joined Kadam monastic training with mahamudra meditation, and his Jewel Ornament of Liberation is still studied as a guide to the stages of the path.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Milarepa's last teaching, his calluses, and no secret beyond practice. Your line: that's the secret.

Before he was anyone's student, he was the doctor. Gampopa trained in medicine, and he's still remembered as the physician from Dakpo, the region where he later taught. He had a wife and a household. Then, the story says, sickness came, and his wife died, and the doctor couldn't save her. Grief turned him toward the teaching. He became a monk and studied hard, until one day he overheard some beggars talking about a yogi in the mountains named Milarepa, and he couldn't let the name go.
screen: `THE PHYSICIAN FROM DAKPO.` → `A LOSS HE COULDN'T HEAL.` → `A NAME OVERHEARD.`

segments.voice: As a monk, Gampopa trained in the Kadam tradition, the one that came down from Atisha. That's the lamp we met last week: careful monastic discipline and the stages of the path, step by step, from the small aim to the great one. Then he walked to Milarepa, the green-skinned singer in the caves, and received the direct meditation teachings Milarepa had from Marpa, Marpa from Naropa, and Naropa from Tilopa. Kagyu teachers call the heart of this mahamudra, the great seal: resting the mind and seeing its own nature directly. Two very different worlds. One is a monastery with rules, texts and a graded curriculum. The other is a cave with a hermit who sings. Gampopa didn't pick one and drop the other. He brought them together. Kagyu teachers describe his tradition as the meeting of two streams, Kadam and mahamudra, and his book, the Jewel Ornament of Liberation, lays the stages of the path out in order for a student who also meditates in the mountain style. Lineages descended from his students carry the Kagyu teaching on, so the line that began with Tilopa runs through him. In Gampopa's joining, the monastery gives the cave its order, and the cave gives the monastery its meditation. Not either-or, but both, each keeping the other honest.
screen: `STREAM ONE: ATISHA'S KADAM.` · `STREAM TWO: MILAREPA'S MAHAMUDRA.` · `THE MONASTERY MEETS THE CAVE.` · `NOT EITHER-OR, BUT BOTH.` · then, large: `TWO STREAMS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind two things you love that rarely sit together, running and prayer, cooking and music, work and a friend, and hold one in each hand, so to speak. Ask what it would look like to bring them together, even once, and let a picture come as you rest in the breath.
Gampopa. The physician who became a monk, studied with Milarepa, and joined Atisha's stages of the path with mahamudra in the Kagyu school. Today's word.
Your line: two streams. The monastery and the cave, each giving the other what it lacked. See you at the next step.

977.title: Machig Labdrön
977.hook: the Tibetan woman teacher who, tradition says, founded chöd, offering the body to fear
977.howItsDone: Chöd is practiced in Tibetan Buddhist communities, usually after receiving it from a teacher, with chanted liturgy, a hand drum and bell, and a visualized offering of the body; some practitioners do it in lonely or frightening places.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Gampopa, the doctor who became a monk. Your line: two streams.

A burial ground at night, high on the Tibetan plateau. Wind, a scatter of bones, a small hand drum in one hand and a bell in the other. Someone sits down in the one place everyone else walks around, and does it on purpose. Tradition traces this practice to a woman named Machig Labdrön, a reader of the Perfection of Wisdom sutras who became a teacher with students of her own. What she taught sounds backward at first: walk toward the thing that frightens you, and offer it a meal.
screen: `A BURIAL GROUND AT NIGHT.` → `A DRUM AND A BELL.` → `WALK TOWARD THE FEAR.`

segments.voice: First, the name of her practice: chöd, a Tibetan word meaning to cut. What gets cut is not a person, and not really a demon. In her teaching, the true demon is the grip of the self, the habit of clutching at me and mine, and fear is where that grip shows itself most plainly. Second, the method. In the visualization, the practitioner imagines leaving the body behind and offering it as food and nectar to every hungry being, the gentle guests and the frightening ones alike. Nothing is held back. The point is not to act brave. It is to stop guarding the very thing fear is trying to protect. Third, the root. Machig's practice rests on the Perfection of Wisdom sutras, which teach that nothing has a separate, solid self. Chöd takes that teaching off the page and into the dark: if there is no solid self, whatever the demon eats was never really owned. Fourth, a woman's lineage. Her life stories describe a teacher who had a family, raised children, and gathered students, and tradition says her teaching even traveled from Tibet back to India, a stream flowing the other way. Chöd is still practiced in Tibetan Buddhism, often with the drum and bell, and it is traditionally received from a teacher after preparation. It is not a dare. It is generosity, aimed at the thing you'd rather run from.
screen: `CHÖD: CUTTING THE GRIP OF SELF.` · `OFFER THE BODY TO EVERY HUNGRY BEING.` · `THE PERFECTION OF WISDOM, IN THE DARK.` · `A WOMAN'S LINEAGE.` · then, large: `GENEROSITY AIMED AT FEAR.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small fear, not the biggest one, a phone call you keep putting off or a worry about a bill, and notice where it shows up in the body. Don't push it away, and don't feed the story; turn toward it the way you'd turn toward a guest at the door, letting your hands open a little on each out-breath. If it grows too big, come back to the breath alone.
Machig Labdrön. The Tibetan teacher whom tradition credits with chöd, cutting the grip of self by offering it to fear. Today's word.
Your line: offer it to fear. Whatever it eats was never really yours to guard. Day nine hundred seventy-seven, done.

978.title: Yeshe Tsogyal
978.hook: honored as Padmasambhava's closest student and a great teacher herself
978.howItsDone: In the Nyingma school, Yeshe Tsogyal is honored in prayers and visualizations alongside Padmasambhava, her life story is read and taught, and Nyingma practitioners receive teachings from treasure texts that tradition says she helped conceal.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Machig Labdrön and chöd, cutting the grip of self. Your line: offer it to fear.

A small yellow scroll, rolled tight, pressed into a crack in a cliff and sealed over with stone. Nobody is meant to find it this year, or the next. In Tibetan tradition, some teachings were hidden like this on purpose, the stories say, waiting for the right person at the right time. And the one who wrote many of them down and helped hide them, the stories say, was a woman. She is honored as Padmasambhava's student and companion, and as a teacher in her own right. Today, Yeshe Tsogyal.
screen: `A SCROLL IN A CLIFF.` → `HIDDEN ON PURPOSE.` → `A WOMAN WROTE THEM DOWN.`

segments.voice: First, who she is in the story. Tibetan tradition remembers her as a young noblewoman who wanted a life of practice more than the marriage planned for her. In time she became the student, and the consort, of Padmasambhava, the teacher from India whom Tibetans call Guru Rinpoche. Second, the keeper of the words. Tradition says she held his teachings in memory, wrote them in a coded script, and hid them as terma, treasures, so that later teachers, called treasure finders, could reveal them when people were ready. In this way of seeing, a teaching can wait for its listener. Third, a teacher herself. Her life story tells of long retreats in caves and snow, of hardship, of healing the sick, and of students of her own, who kept learning from her after Padmasambhava left Tibet. She is not only the one who listened; she is also the one who taught. Fourth, the great mother. In the Nyingma school, Yeshe Tsogyal is honored as wisdom itself in a woman's form. Her devotees connect her with the Perfection of Wisdom, which Buddhist texts call the mother of all Buddhas, and so with the great mother. That title is not about having children. It is about wisdom as the source from which awakening is born. Different Tibetan schools hold her in different degrees of devotion, and these stories come chiefly from the Nyingma tradition.

979.title: Sakya Pandita
979.hook: the scholar of the Sakya school, famous for his book of wise sayings
979.howItsDone: In Tibetan communities, verses from Sakya Pandita's Treasury of Good Sayings are learned and quoted, and his work on logic is studied in monastic settings, especially in the Sakya school.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Yeshe Tsogyal, keeper of the hidden teachings. Your line: the great mother.

Measure twice, cut once. Don't go to bed angry. Some families have a few lines like that, said by a grandmother so often that they stuck, and years later they come out of a grandchild's mouth at the oddest moments. Tibet has a book of lines like that, short verses of good sense, small enough to learn by heart. The man who wrote it was a celebrated scholar, a master of logic and debate. And he chose to put a lot of what he knew into sayings small enough to carry. Today, Sakya Pandita.
screen: `LINES THAT GET PASSED DOWN.` → `A TIBETAN BOOK OF GOOD SENSE.` → `A SCHOLAR WHO WROTE SMALL.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Sakya is a school of Tibetan Buddhism, named for the monastery at its center. Pandita is a Sanskrit title for a learned scholar; tradition says Tibetans gave him that title because he mastered the Indian sciences, from grammar to logic. He also wrote a work on logic, the Treasury of Valid Reasoning. Second, the surprise. This same scholar wrote the Treasury of Good Sayings, short verses about everyday life: how the wise and the foolish behave, how to treat friends, how to hold wealth, how to speak. The verses lean on everyday pictures, from the house, the field and the road. Third, why a scholar would write this way. A long argument helps a student in the debating courtyard. A short saying goes home with the farmer and the trader, and comes back to mind when it's needed. One saying credited to him runs roughly like this: even if you will die tomorrow, study today; you may not become wise in this life, but it is like saving wealth for the next. Fourth, his life outside the library. Tradition says that late in life he traveled to the court of a Mongol prince, and that his teaching there helped shape how Mongol rulers and Tibetan teachers dealt with each other afterward. The man who wrote about speaking well, the story goes, was asked to practice it in a foreign court, far from home.

980.title: Longchenpa
980.hook: the great Nyingma writer on the mind's natural state
980.howItsDone: In the Nyingma school, students traditionally complete preliminary practices before a teacher introduces the mind's nature, and Longchenpa's Treasuries are studied in monastic colleges and retreat settings as guides to Dzogchen.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sakya Pandita, the scholar who wrote small. Your line: wise sayings. Today closes a week.

Take a glass of stream water, cloudy with silt. Stir it to hurry it clean, and it only gets cloudier. Set it on the windowsill and walk away, and slowly the silt settles on its own, and the water is clear. Nobody made it clear. It was clear water all along, with something stirred into it. Tibetan teachers use pictures like this for a teaching about the mind, and one writer in the Nyingma school wrote about that teaching in pages his school still treasures. Today, Longchenpa.
screen: `CLOUDY WATER, STIRRED.` → `LEFT ALONE, IT CLEARS.` → `CLEAR ALL ALONG.`

segments.voice: First, the writer. Longchenpa belongs to the Nyingma, the school that traces itself to Padmasambhava. Tradition remembers him as a scholar who spent long stretches in retreat, and who wrote a set of works known as the Treasuries, which Nyingma students still study. Second, the teaching he wrote about: Dzogchen, the Great Perfection. Its claim is startling. The mind's own nature is already awake: open like the sky, clear like a lamp, warm with care. It doesn't need to be built. Thoughts and moods pass through it the way clouds pass through the sky, and the sky is never stained. Third, the method, which is almost no method. If the natural state is already here, then effort to manufacture it gets in the way, like stirring the glass. Longchenpa's writing keeps returning to this: don't fabricate, don't fix, leave it as it is. Fourth, the care around it. Nyingma teachers say this natural state is pointed out by a teacher, and that resting without effort is not the same as drifting or dozing. Traditionally, students prepare first. The ease is real, but it's not cheap. And a look back at this week: the nettles and the last teaching of Milarepa, Gampopa joining two streams, Machig offering fear a meal, Yeshe Tsogyal hiding treasure, Sakya Pandita's sayings, and now Longchenpa, telling the mind to stop stirring its own water.
screen: `A NYINGMA WRITER OF THE TREASURIES.` · `DZOGCHEN: THE MIND ALREADY AWAKE.` · `DON'T FABRICATE. LEAVE IT AS IT IS.` · `POINTED OUT BY A TEACHER.` · then, large: `THE NATURAL STATE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, breathing however the body wants, with nothing to achieve for one minute. Let thoughts and sounds come and go without chasing them or pushing them out. If you catch yourself trying hard to rest, let even the trying settle, like the glass on the windowsill.
Longchenpa. The Nyingma writer of the Treasuries, who taught Dzogchen: the mind's natural state is already awake, and rest, not effort, lets it show. Today's word.
Your line: natural state. Clear all along, once the stirring stops. Day nine hundred eighty, and a week complete.

fork.setup: you sit to rest your mind, and thoughts keep arriving. what would Longchenpa's teaching suggest?
options: push them out by force
follow each one to its end

fork.reveal: Dzogchen teaching says thoughts pass like clouds through a sky that is never stained. leave them as they are.

chat.says: If my mind is already awake, why does it feel so messy?
options: Like stirred water: stop stirring and the silt settles; it was clear all along.
Each passing thought stains the mind for good, so it stays cloudy.
Resting just means dozing off, and sleep is what clears the water.
chat.meaning: In Dzogchen, thoughts pass through the mind like clouds through the sky, and the sky is never stained. Effort to manufacture clarity is the stirring.
